Brown Act

Agendas are drafted to accurately state what the legislative body is being asked to consider. The
legislative body can take action on "all items" listed on the agenda and be in compliance with the open
meeting laws. Under the Brown Act, no action may be taken on a matter unless it is listed on the
agenda, or unless certain emergency or special circumstances exist. The governing body may direct
staff to investigate and/or schedule certain matters for consideration at a future meeting.

GENERAL NOTICE TO THE PUBLIC

The City Council adopted new rules relating to the conduct of the public meetings, proceedings, and
business in the City of South Gate on July 12, 2022, (Resolution 2022-38-CC) and go into effect on
August 1, 2022. Resolution #2022-38-CC is available at the City Clerk’s Office.

MEETING SCHEDULE

Regular meetings of the City Council are held on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month, closed
session meetings will commence at 5:30 p.m. unless posted otherwise on its agenda. The regular City
Council meetings will commence at 6:30 p.m. Agendas are available at the following locations: City Clerk

  6
 Office, Public Notice Boards at City Hall, and on the City’s web page at https://www.cityofsouthgate.org

The Public can sign up to receive automatic notices of postings of agendas for the City Council or any
other Commission or Board of the City of South Gate. Visit the City webpage and click on the Agenda &
Minutes icon. That will take you the page where an individual can enter their email in the “Email
Updates” box to register.

PUBLIC COMMENT/PARTICIPATION

Any person may request to address a legislative body during a public meeting. The Presiding Officer will
call upon those present in the Council Chambers.

Speakers are limited to three (3) minutes on any item listed on the agenda, including public hearings.
Under Comments from the Audience portion, speakers are also limited to a single three (3) minutes time
limit. Comments from the Audience is initially limited to 45 minutes at each meeting. Any speaker still
wishing to speak, that did not speak, will have an addition Comments from the Audience opportunity after
the last business item is finished. The Presiding Officer may extend the time limit as long as there is no
objection from the City Council as a body.

To ensure that the public is able to participate, the City provides the opportunity to submit their
comments in person, email, mail. Methods of participation may be subject to change during other such
times when a State of Emergency, Health Order or State Executive Order limits in-person participation.

CURFEW

In absence of a motion duly adopted by majority vote of the City Council, the Presiding Officer may
adjourn the City Council meetings at 10:30 p.m. The Presiding Officer may ask the City Council if any
agenda items listed should be continued or dealt with during the meeting. For those items to be
continued, the City Council can direct the item be placed on the next City Council agenda or the current
meeting may be adjourned to a time certain at which time the meeting shall be reconvened as an
Adjourned Regular Meeting of the City Council and action upon the published agenda continued.

STAFF REPORTS

As a general rule, staff reports. or other written documentation are prepared/organized with respect to
each item of business listed on the agenda. Meeting agendas and staff reports are available at least 72-
hours prior to the scheduled regular City Council meeting and a minimum of 24-hours prior to a Special
City Council meeting. There are times when the City Council receives written material. revised material
after the posting of agendas, these materials are become a public record and will be available for public
view within 72-hours after the meeting in which they were received. Those materials and any other public
document can be inspected in the City Clerk's Office located at 8650 California Avenue, South Gate.

SERVICES TO FACILITATE ACCESS TO PUBLIC MEETINGS

In compliance with the American with Disabilities Act, if you need special assistance to participate in the
City Council Meetings, please contact the Office of the City Clerk. Notification 48 hours prior to the City
Council Meeting will enable the City to make reasonable arrangements to assure accessibility. For
further information, please contact the Office of the City Clerk at (323) 563-9510 or via email at
yglaze@sogate.org.

OF THE  SOUTH  GATE  MUNICIPAL  CODE

PURPOSE:  To adopt  Ordinance  No.  2025-01-CC  to amend  Title  11, Chapter  11.43  (Accessory
Dwelling  Units  and Accessory  Structures)  to comply  with  state law updates.

RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City  Council  will  consider:

  a.  Waiving  the reading  in full  and adopting  Ordinance  No. 2025-01-OCC,  amending  Title  11,
  Chapter  11.43  (Accessory  Dwelling  Units  and Accessory  Structures)  of the  South  Gate
  Municipal  Code;  and
  b.  Accepting  the determination  that the proposed  amendment  is Exempt  from  the California
  Environmental  Quality  Act  ("CEQA")  as a "ministerial"  project  pursuant  to  CEQA
  Guidelines  Section  15268(a).

PUBLIC  NOTIFICATION:  Advertising  and notification  of the public  hearing  were conducted  in
compliance  with  Chapter  11.50.020  of the South  Gate Municipal  Code.  Notice  of the hearing  was
posted  and published  in the "South  Gate Press"  newspaper  on August  28, 2025.

ENVIRONMENTAL  EXEMPTION:  The City  of South Gate has determined  that the zoning  code
amendment  is exempt  from  CEQA  as a "ministerial"  project  pursuant  to CEQA  Guidelines  Section
15268(a).  Ordinance  No.  2025-01-CC  would  modify  development  standards  and  approval
requirements  for Accessory  Dwelling  Units  (ADUs)  in compliance  with  existing  State law,  which
establishes  that ADUs  are ministerial  projects.

FISCAL  IMPACT:  There  is no fiscal  impact  to the General  Fund for the recommended  action.

BACKGROUND:  In January  2021, the City  of South  Gate established  Chapter  11.43  of the South
Gate Municipal  Code  (SGMC),  which  allowed  Accessory  Dwelling  Units  (ADUs)  as required  by
Government  Code Section  66323,  previously  referred  to as "granny  flats",  "in-law  suite"  or "rumpus
rooms".  Since  this  time,  the  State  law  regarding  ADUs  and Junior  Accessory  Dwelling  Units
(JADUs)  has continued  to be modified  as new bills  are signed  into  law by the Governor,  such as

  OFFICE  OF EMERGENCY  SERVICES  ("CAL  OES")  FOR THE  EMERGENCY
  OPERATION  CENTER ("EOC")  PROJECT,  CITY PROJECT  N0. 582-ARC

  PURPOSE:  City Council approval is requested to accept $1,226,000 in grant funds from the
  California Governor's Office of Emergency Services and to allocate $408,667 in General Funds
  as the required local match for the Emergency Operations Center (EOC) Project. These actions
  will fully fund the $1,634,667 project budget. Approval will allow the City to relocate the EOC
  to a modern, reliable, and accessible facility at the Civic Center.

  RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City Council will consider:
  a. Accepting  $1,226,000  in grant funds from the California  Governor's Office of
  Emergency  Services (Cal OES) and appropriating  the funds to the Emergency
  Operations  Center (EOC) Project, City Project No. 582-ARC; and
  b.  Transferring $100,000 in AQMD Funds and $308,667 from Building Infrastructure
  and Maintenance  Fund (BIM)  to the Emergency Operations Center (EOC) City
  Project No. 582-ARC, to fully fund the project.

  FISCAL  IMPACT:  The grant application requests $1,226,000 and requires a $408,667 local
  match,  resulting  in a total  project budget of $1,634,667.  The local match will be funded by
  transferring $100,000 in AQMD  Funds and $308,667 from Building  Infrastrueture and
  Maintenance  Fund (BIM) to the Emergency Operations Center (EOC) City Project No. 582-
  ARC, to fully fund the project.

  ANALYSIS:  On February 25, 2025, the City Council adopted a Resolution authorizing the
  submission  of a grant application to Cal OES for the design and construction  of a new
  Emergency  Operations Center (EOC). Cal OES subsequently approved the application and
  allocated $1,226,000 in grant funds to the project.

  The  grant  was  originally  approved with the requirement  that the facility  be located at the South
  Gate Courthouse (8640 California  Avenue). However, due to feasibility  issuesi including
  asbestos  abatement, seismic  retrofitting,  and limited parking, the City requested approval to
  relocate  the project. On June 5, 2025, Cal OES approved the amendment to change the location
  to 8680 California  Avenue, within the Civic Center Museum, where the EOC will be
  incorporated  into a dual-purpose space that functions year-round as a museum and community
  1

  36
 room  while  serving  as the EOC  during  emergencies.  This  new  location  provides  a more  cost-
effective  and  practical  solution  while  ensuring  the  City  has a modern,  reliable,  and  accessible
facility  to support  emergency  operations.  By  accepting  the grant  'funds,  the Council  commits  to
fully  funding  the  project  and  authorizing  the  conversion  of  the  museum  into  a dual-purpose
facility.

Design  is scheduled  to begin  in December  of 2025  and  is expected  to be completed  within  six
months.  Construction  will  follow  and is anticipated  to require  six to eight  months  to complete.

BACKGROUND:  The  South  Gate  Police  Station,  built  in  1948,  houses  an  Emergency
Operations  Center  ("EOC")  in a subterranean  section  of the building.  Tis  location  is prone  to
flooding,  lacks  ADA-compliant  access,  and  faces  significant  communication  challenges  due  to
the thick  concrete  walls.  Given  that  effective  communication  is critical  for  emergency  response,
staff  recommended  relocating  the EOC  to ensure  reliable  operations  during  major  events.

The  project  relocates  the existing  EOC  from  the  SGPD  basement  to a new  facility  at the  Civic
Center  by repurposing  a portion  of the museum  to meet  modern  EOC  requirements.  The  section
of  the  museum  is planned  to  serve  a dual  purpose:  an  as-needed  EOC  and  a Community
Room/Museum.  Daily,  the improved  section  will  serve  as a conference  room,  community  room
and a museum.  However,  when  the EOC  is activated,  that  will  be shut down  to the public  and the
EOC  will  be activated.  Some  of the displays  in this  portion  of the museum  that  will  be removed
will  be relocated  to the easterly  side  of the museum  section.  They  will  continue  to be available
for public  viewing  to a practical  extent.  Other  displays  will  be integrated  into  the room,  keeping
part  of the museum  experience  while  still  allotting  appropriate  space  for the EOC  needs.

As  a note,  the  originally  proposed  relocation  was  to  8640  California  Avenue  (South  Gate
Courthouse).  However,  that  presented  significant  challenges,  including  asbestos  removal,
seismic  retrofitting  to comply  with  the  2024  Building  Code,  and  insufficient  staff  parking.  The
Civic  Center  location  avoids  these  issues,  making  it a more  suitable  choice  for the new  EOC.

The proposed  budget  is $1,634,667.  Work  includes,  but is not limited  to, upgrading  electrical  and
mechanical  systems  for  proper  heating  and  air conditioning,  a backup  generator,  equipping  the
space  with  televisions,  tables,  computers,  desks,  radios,  and  cell  phones  to support  emergency
operations.  The proposed  budget  will  be expended  as sumrffiarized  below.

 SUBJECT:  CHANGE  ORDER  NO.  l WITH  CALIFORNIA  COMMERCIAL  POOLS
 FOR  EMERGENCY  REPAIRS  AT  THF,  PATRICIA  G. MITCHELL  SWIM  ST ADIUM
 AND  APPROPRIATION  TO REPLENISH  POOL  MAINTENANCE  FUNDS

 PURPOSE:  The Patricia  G. Mitchell  Swim  Stadium  recently  experienced  equipment  failures
 that required  immediate  emergency  repairs  to keep the facility  safe and open to the public.  While
 completing  these repairs,  additional  deficiencies  were discovered  that added $63,225  in costs but
 needed to be addressed  while  the pool was drained  to avoid prolonged  closure  and higher  expenses.

 This report  also seeks to replenish  the pool  maintenance  budget  so that scheduled  repair  projects
 for this fiscal  year can still move  forward.

 RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City  Council  will  consider:

  a. Authorizing  the City  Manager  to approve  Change  Order  No. 1 to Purchase  Order  with
  California  Commercial  Pools  to :[und emergency  repairs  at the Patricia  G. Mitchell  Swim
  Stadium,  in an amount  not to exceed  $63,225;  and

  b. Appropriating  $104,025  from  the  General  Fund  to replenish  the  FY  2025/26  Pool
  Maintenance  Budget  as needed  to fund planned  repairs.

 FISCAL  IMPACT:  Change  Order  No. 1 to Purchase  Order  with  California  Commercial  Pools
 is in the amount  of $63,225  and will  be funded  with  General  Funds.  With  this change,  the revised
 purchase  order  total  is $104,025,  fully  funded  by  General  Funds.  The  total  appropriation  to
 replenish  the Pool Maintenance  Budget  for planned  repairs  is $104,025  from  the General  Fund.

 ANALYSIS:  The  City  operates  the Patricia  G. Mitchell  Swim  Stadium,  a major  community
 facility  that supports  year-round  aquatics  programming.  Recently,  critical  pool  equipment  failed,
 requiring  immediate  attention  to maintain  safe operations  and avoid  disruption  to public  use.

 Initially,  the City  issued  Purchase  Order  with  California  Commercial  Pools  in the amount  of
 $40,800  to address  several  identified  pool  facility  issues.  To ensure  accuracy,  Myrtha  Pools,  the
 manufacturer  of the existing  pool system,  was contacted  to evaluate  the reported  conditions.  Based
 on their  assessment,  a repair  scope was developed  in coordination  with  California  Commercial
 Pools,  a Myrtha-authorized  contractor.

 As work  commenced  and the pool was drained,  additional  urgent  deficiencies  were discovered  that
required  immediate  repairs.  Performing  these repairs  while  the pool  remained  empty  was critical
to  minimize  costs,  avoid  extended  downtime,  and  ensure  continuity  of  programming.  The
additional  work  totaled  approximately  $63,225.

The original  $40,800  scope included  replacing  damaged  tile targets,  repairing  the pool wall
membrane,  painting  new targets,  replacing  broken  piping  and valves,  installing  new pump
plumbing,  providing  a temporary  anchor,  and site cleanup.  The $63,225  emergency  work  added
replacement  of five  butterfly  valves,  a new float  valve  and floats,  three valve  extensions,  repairs
to four wall  seals, waterproofing  of penetrations,  and site cleanup.  Staff is requesting  the City
Manager  be authorized  to approve  Change  Order  No.  I to Purchase  Order  to fully  fund the
completed  repairs.

BACKGROUND:  The  Patricia  G. Mitchell  Swim  Stadium  is undergoing  scheduled  repairs
funded  through  the FY  2025/26  pool  maintenance  budget.  Maintenance  staff  initially  identified
several  priority  issues  requiring  attention.  Myrtha  Pools  was contacted  to inspect  the pool  and
helped  develop  a detailed  repair  scope,  which  was awarded  to California  Commercial  Pools,  a
certified  Myrtha  contractor.

During  the repair  process,  additional  critical  issues were discovered,  particularly  in the surge pit
and pump  pit.  These  included  deteriorated  valves,  failed  float  controls,  and compromised  wall
penetrations.  Because  these conditions  posed  a threat  to pool  operations  and delayed  reopening,
the City  Manager  approved  emergency  continuation.

This staff report  now  seeks Council  to authorize  the City  Manager  to approve  Change  Order  No.
l to Purchase  Order  with  California  Commercial  Pools  in the amount  of $63,225  to fully  fund the
completed  repairs.

The $115,000 pool  maintenance  budget  in the FY 2025/26  0perating  Budget  for plaru'ied  repairs
was utilized  to complete  these  emergency  repairs.  The  original  $115,000  appropriation  was
specifically  earmarked  for critical  system  equipment  replacement,  which  must  still  be completed
during  this fiscal  year. As such, an appropriation  in the amount  of $104,025  in General  Funds  is
needed to fully  'fund the $115,000  pool  maintenance  budget.

CITY OF SOUTH GATE
  REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING
  MINUTES
  TUESDAY, OCTOBER 14, 2025

CALL TO ORDER  Maria Davila, Mayor called a Regular City Council Meeting to order at
  6:33 p.m.

INVOCATION  Bishop Juan Carlos Mendez
PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE  Yodit Glaze, City Clerk
ROLL CALL  Yodit Glaze, City Clerk

PRESENT  Mayor Maria Davila, Vice Mayor Joshua Barron, Council Member Maria
  del Pilar Avalos Council Member Gil Hurtado and Council Member Al
  Rios; City Treasurer Jose De La Paz, City Manager Rob Houston, City
  Attorney Raúl F. Salinas

1
PRESENTATION  The City Council recognized Retiring Police Chief, Darren Arakawa.

2
SCHOOLS/EDUCATION  The City Council unanimously received and filed a presentation on the
  Proposed Implementation of School Traffic Plan for the 2025-2026 School
  Year by motion of Council Member Davila and seconded by Council
  Member Hurtado.

  ROLL CALL: Council Member Avalos, yes; Council Member Hurtado,
  yes; Council Member Rios, yes; Vice Mayor Barron, yes; Mayor Davila,
  yes.

COMMENTS FROM THE
AUDIENCE – NON-AGENDA
ITEMS  Pablo Cifuentes, volunteers at the South Gate JAA, stated being asked to
  leave the fields at South Gate Park by city staff.

  Mario Sanchez, coach and volunteer for AYSO, inquired about lighting at
  Hollydale Park. He has noticed the baseball fields at South Gate Park are
  empty 90% of the time and if there could be a resolution to the issue.

  Brenda works for The Office of Durango Mexico and is concerned about a
  business next door that is opened 24/7 with questionable clientele. She
  mentioned an incident at that business and congratulated Chief Arakawa
  for great response from the Police Officers.
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF OCTOBER 14, 2025

COMMENTS FROM THE
AUDIENCE – NON-AGENDA
ITEMS  Maria Herrera and others in the audience are present tonight with Casa
  Durango stated they do not feel safe anymore with that certain business
  that is open 24/7. They are saddened Chief Arakawa is retiring and hope
  they will be left in good hands.

  Evelyn, AYSO inquired about lighting at Hollydale Park. She mentioned a
  few grants the City of South Gate has received.

  Esperanza Perez has over fifteen years of service as a social worker, six
  years as a license clinical social worker working with veterans. She served
  eight years in the army. Ms. Perez volunteers as a coach in the AYSO
  soccer league and inquired about the lack of lighting at Hollydale Park.

  Manuel Carrillo experienced a life-changing injury a month ago. He
  demanded and instigated action on park safety and maintenance,
  affordable recreational activities, and equitable healthcare access.

  Nelson Hermosillo, 10135 Dorothy Ave., was not happy with certain
  Council Members behavior at the last City Council Meeting. A certain
  Council Member had concerns about the City’s budget which should be
  addressed.

EMAILS  Mario Dominguez stated that the Tweedy Mile Advisory Board has failed
  to meet twice in a row and is asking City Council to review their
  appointments. He is also asking City Council to consider reducing the
  Citizens Advisory Committee from 20 to 10 members to ensure quorum.
  He is also asking for an update on the fiber optic project.

  Claudia Rivera expressed disappointment with Council Member Rios who
  did not support a raise for SEIU represented city employees. She noted
  that as a union member herself she expected his support.

REPORTS AND COMMENTS
FROM CITY OFFICIALS  Arturo Cervantes, Director of Public Works, stated no updates.

  Steve Costley, Director of Parks and Recreation, stated that AYSO was
  founded in South Gate in 1993 and has always been at Hollydale Regional
  Park and for almost 32 years it has never had lights except for an
  experiment last year which didn’t sufficient lighting. The program was
  more of a summer based to start getting the kids ready for the weekend
  and whatever time frame the city could offer. As to the concept of lights at
  Hollydale Regional Park, it is in the master plan of which the city is
  asking for grant funding to get design for from the Recreation and Open
  Space District for the County of Los Angeles. The estimate for Phase 1 is
  close to 20 million dollars.

  Page 2 of 7
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF OCTOBER 14, 2025

REPORTS AND COMMENTS
FROM CITY OFFICIALS
CONT’D  Mr. Costley stated that as to the question about grant funding, none of the
  grant funding that the city currently receive was designated for Hollydale
  Regional Park. It was designated for Hollydale Community Park. The
  funding was either Prop 68 or state mandated funding that came from
  Assembly Member Rendon’s Office.

  Mr. Costley stated the grand opening at Circle Park went well and thanked
  the county, state, and RMC for all their help.

  Mayor Davila asked City Manager to explain to the audience how the city
  receives grants and how they are used.

  Rob Houston, City Manager, stated it is very complicated to apply for
  funding for any type of project. There are many agencies and cities
  competing for funds. The city has done an amazing job in getting funding
  but the amount of need in the community is always greater than the
  amount of funds. The funds would not be used or available for revamping
  an existing park or adding lights at a park. The funds have limitations on
  what they might be used at.

  Mr. Houston explained that most of the park’s property is not the city. It
  belongs to the Southern California Edison due to the powerlines.

  Gabriel Perez, Director of Community Development, stated no updates.

  Luis Frausto, Director of Administration Services, stated no updates.

  Jon Hamilton, Director of Human Resources, stated no updates.

  Darren Arakawa, Chief of Police, addressed the issue with 9825 Long
  Beach Blvd., and stated that the police department is aware of that
  location.

  Rob Houston, City Manager, stated that the city had a Police Chief
  recruitment that has been occurring over the last several months. Captain
  Manny Arana was offered the job as Police Chief.

  Darren Arakawa, Chief of Police, announced that tomorrow will be the
  final roll call for him and then the transition of the Office of the Chief of
  Police. He will be very happy and proud to put the badge on Captain
  Arana.

  Manny Arana, Police Captain, thanked everyone for their support for the
  position as Police Chief.

  Raúl F. Salinas, City Attorney, congratulated the new Police Chief.

  Page 3 of 7
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF OCTOBER 14, 2025

REPORTS AND COMMENTS
FROM CITY OFFICIALS
CONT’D  Jose De La Paz, City Treasurer, congratulated the new Police Chief.

  Yodit Glaze, City Clerk, congratulated the new Police Chief. She also
  introduced Lindsay Sanavria, Southeast High school student. Ms. Sanavria
  was interested in shadowing Mr. Glaze during a Council Meeting.

  Council Member Avalos welcomed the New Chief of Police and farewell
  to Police Chief Arakawa.

  Council Member Avalos attended the League of Cities’ yearly expo in
  Long Beach. She attended several workshops that focused on good
  governance, fiscal responsibility and strategies for addressing municipal
  deficits. She also attended a community recognition dinner honoring
  several nonprofit organizations in the Southeast Los Angeles area,
  including the YMCA and SELA Kiwanis. She had the privilege of
  attending the grand reopening of Circle Park and thanked Steve Costely,
  Director of Parks & Recreation.

  Council Member Avalos spoke about new legislation, specifically SB707
  coming into effect July 1, 2026, SB79, which is a transit-oriented housing
  development upzoning which will make it faster and easier to build
  multifamily units. She reminded everyone to vote.

  Council Member Hurtado is concerned about SB707 due to the change in
  the new law which states if the system is disrupted, the legislative body
  must recess for at least one hour and if the system does not come on the
  meeting continues but if someone was going to call in, it wont be possible.

  Council Member Hurtado is glad that some of the AYSO issues were
  addressed. He attended the grand opening of Circle Park.

  Council Member Rios stated the city needs to find a resolution for AYSO.
  He mentioned cities that have call-in features, and this city should have
  one too.

  Council Member Rios thanked Vice Mayor Barron as the President for
  SELA Kiwanis and the SELA Kiwanis for the event on September 30th.

  Vice Mayor Barron stated that for the last two months, he has been
  working on how to solve the AYSO problem. He is concerned regarding
  the state’s mandates to have properties being built up to 6 feet.
